ozet: Abraha, the Abyssinian commander in Yemen, marches on Mecca to destroy the Ka'ba; 'Abd al-Muttalib's stance, the elephant that kneels, and the birds. The episode ends with the Year of the Elephant.

b02-s01: Far to the south of Mecca, in Yemen, the Abyssinians were in power.
At their head was Abraha. Because of a wound to his face from a battle, he was called 'al-Ashram', the one with the split face.
He was a short, stout man, firmly devoted to Christianity.
b02-s02: In San'a, Abraha built a church the like of which had never been seen.
Then he wrote to the Abyssinian king, the Negus: he would not rest until he had turned the pilgrimage of the Arabs to this church.
b02-s03: When the news spread, a man of the tribe of Kinana was angered. He went to San'a, entered the church, defiled it, and returned home.
When Abraha learned of this, he was furious. He swore to march on the Ka'ba and destroy it.
b02-s04: Abraha made the Abyssinians ready and set out, taking an elephant with him.
The Arabs saw this as a great danger. When they heard that he meant to destroy the Ka'ba, they felt it was their duty to resist him.
b02-s05: Dhu Nafar, a nobleman of Yemen, gathered his people and fought Abraha; he was defeated and taken prisoner. Abraha did not kill him but kept him with him in bonds.
In the land of the Khath'am tribe, Nufayl ibn Habib also resisted. He too was defeated, and in return for his life he agreed to guide Abraha.
b02-s06: As the army passed Ta'if, Mas'ud ibn Mu'attib of the Thaqif tribe submitted to Abraha.
They asked that the house of their own idol, al-Lat, be left alone; telling him that the house he sought was the one in Mecca, they gave him Abu Righal to show him the way.
Abu Righal died when the army camped at al-Mughammas near Mecca. In later times the Arabs would stone his grave.
b02-s07: From al-Mughammas, Abraha sent the Abyssinian al-Aswad ibn Maqsud with horsemen to Mecca.
Al-Aswad drove off the livestock of Quraysh and the people of Tihama. Among them were two hundred camels belonging to 'Abd al-Muttalib, then the chief of Quraysh.
Quraysh, Kinana and Hudhayl thought of fighting, but realised they were not strong enough and gave up the idea.
b02-s08: Abraha sent Hunata the Himyarite to Mecca: he had not come to fight, only to destroy this house; if they did not resist, he would not shed their blood.
'Abd al-Muttalib replied: they did not wish to fight him, nor did they have the strength to.
This was the sacred House of Allah, the house of His friend Abraham. If He protected it, He would be protecting His own house; if He left it, they had no strength to defend it.
b02-s09: 'Abd al-Muttalib went to Abraha's camp with some of his sons.
His friend Dhu Nafar, the prisoner, asked Unays, the keeper of the elephant, to speak for him.
'Abd al-Muttalib was the most handsome and dignified of men. When Abraha saw him, he showed him respect.
He did not want to seat him lower than himself, nor did he want the Abyssinians to see him beside him on the throne. So he came down from his throne, sat on the carpet and seated him at his side.
b02-s10: Abraha asked what he wanted. 'Abd al-Muttalib asked only for the return of his two hundred camels.

Abraha said: he had admired him when he saw him, but had thought less of him once he spoke. He talked of his camels, yet said nothing of the house that was his religion and the religion of his forefathers, which Abraha had come to destroy.
'Abd al-Muttalib said: «I am the owner of the camels. The House, too, has an Owner who will protect it.»
b02-s11: When 'Abd al-Muttalib returned to Mecca, he told Quraysh to leave the town and withdraw to the mountain tops and valleys, to be safe from the army's attack.
Then he took hold of the door ring of the Ka'ba and, together with a few men of Quraysh, prayed to Allah against Abraha and his army.
After that he let go of the ring, withdrew with them to the mountains, and they began to wait.
b02-s12: In the morning Abraha made his army and his elephant ready to enter Mecca. The elephant's name was Mahmud.
As they turned the elephant towards Mecca, Nufayl came up to it and took hold of its ear: «Kneel, Mahmud, and go back safely the way you came, for you are in the sacred land of Allah.»
The elephant knelt. Whatever they did to raise it, it would not get up.
When they turned it towards Yemen, Syria or the east, it walked; when they turned it towards Mecca, it knelt again.
b02-s13: Just then, birds came from the direction of the sea. The birds were carrying stones.
According to the reports, each of these swallow-like birds carried three stones, one in its beak and two in its feet; the stones were the size of chickpeas and lentils.
Whoever was struck by a stone died; but the stones did not strike everyone.
b02-s14: The Qur'an tells of this event:
«Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the owners of the Elephant? Did He not bring their stratagem to nothing,
And send against them swarms of flying creatures, which pelted them with stones of baked clay,
And made them like green crops devoured (by cattle)?»
b02-s15: Those who survived fled back the way they had come; they looked for Nufayl to show them the road back to Yemen. They fell along the roads and were left behind.
Abraha too was wounded. He was carried to San'a, and there he died.
b02-s16: Among the Arabs that year was remembered as 'the Year of the Elephant'. For a time Quraysh counted their dates from it.
The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is held to have been born in this Year of the Elephant, in 571 CE.
Years later, on the road to Hudaybiya, the Messenger of Allah's camel al-Qaswa knelt and would not get up, and people said: «Al-Qaswa has knelt, she will not move.»

The Messenger of Allah said: «No, al-Qaswa has not knelt of her own accord; that is not her nature. But the One who once held back the elephant (of Abraha from Mecca) has now held back al-Qaswa (from entering the town).»
